Selected work

Start here RF telemetry link EPFL Racing Team
Feb – Aug 2026
With one teammate Firmware

A radio link for a race car, where the clock mattered more than the range

The radio link that sends live sensor data from the team's formula student car to a base station, written in C on an RTOS. We expected range to be the hard part. It was not: the real limit was time, because every message has to get across before the next one is ready. We worked it out as a pair and co-wrote the design notes, and the team leads made the final call.

Based on link-budget calculations, not measured on track.

Stitchmeter Mechanism Design II (MICRO-201), EPFL
Spring 2026 · team of 5
Graded 5/6 Mechanical

A surgical suture gauge with no electronics

A purely mechanical device that shows how tightly a stitch is tied and how much pull the knot takes before it slips. There is no sensor and no battery: just thin blades, a lever and a pantograph that magnify tiny movements into a reading you can see.

I built the full 3D CATIA model and assembly. When our first layout did not fit the size limit, I proposed nesting the stages inside one another.

Squash-ball launcher Mechanical design project (ME-102/107), EPFL
Spring 2025 · team of 4
Design only, not built Mechanical

A hand-cranked machine designed to throw a squash ball at 100 km/h

No motor: one person turns a crank, a gear train spins two wheels up to speed, and the wheels grip each ball and throw it. The tricky part was feeding the balls in only once the wheels are fast enough. We designed the whole machine on paper and did not build it.

Digital system on an FPGA Logic Systems, EPFL
Fall 2025 · team of 2 · course grade 5.75/6 Digital logic

A clock, an alarm and a guessing game, built from logic gates on an FPGA

Built with a partner from gates, counters and state machines in Logisim, then loaded onto an Intel FPGA board. One button steps through a clock, an alarm, a stopwatch, a countdown timer and a number-guessing game. Tilting the board, read by its accelerometer, sets the values, and three melodies play from a counter and a small memory.

The hard part was timing. A button press had to move the system exactly one step, so we built edge detectors that fire for a single clock cycle. Giving the counters one clean clock instead of gated clocks also cut the delay.

Four-mode handheld Microcontrollers, EPFL
Spring 2026 · team of 2 Embedded

Thermometer, compass, radar and lamp in AVR assembly

Built with a partner on a small microcontroller, programmed in assembly: an infrared remote switches between a thermometer, a compass, a distance radar and a lamp.

RoboHack 2026 36-hour hardware hackathon
Team of 4 Robotics

A plant-health robot arm that learns from demonstrations

As a team we built a leader arm and a follower arm, showed the follower how to do the job by moving the leader by hand, and trained a model to repeat it. At 2 AM only four of the motors responded. We recalibrated both arms and had it all working by sunrise.

C++ arena game EPFL, Spring 2025
Team of 2 · graded 6/6 Software

A real-time chain game in C++17

Particles drift through a circular arena while the player builds a chain and steers it to collect them. I wrote the code, in C++ with a graphical interface.

Designing a circuit board Course project, CMU
Fall 2026 In progress

What does it take to turn a drawing into a board a factory can make?

A course project on the full path from idea to a real board: I draw the schematic, lay out the board, check it in 3D, and prepare the parts list and placement files for a factory to make it. I soldered the pins that connect the reference board to the Arduino myself, and use the Arduino to test how it behaves.

Not manufactured yet. Nothing here has been built or tested on my own board.

Boeing 737 MAX Feedback Control Systems, CMU
Fall 2026 In progress

Why MCAS failed, and how the fix addressed it

A control-systems final project on the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes. A system that trusted a single sensor was given too much authority, and nothing checked whether the reading was wrong. I compare the faulty and the fixed versions in a simple simulation.

Roadside camera study Planned

Where is a vehicle on the road, in metres, from one fixed camera?

A real-world feasibility study that I plan to take on. Software can already draw a box around a car in a camera image, but a box does not say where the car is on the road. The question is whether one fixed traffic camera can tell us, in metres, without being calibrated by hand.

Not started yet. This describes the plan, not results.
